name: Rentvine

gate1.read: Any Rentvine customer can create an API key on their own and connect the official AI (MCP) connector. There is no sales call, plan upgrade, or extra fee for either.

gate2.read: The API reads nearly everything and handles the core daily writes: creating leases, posting rent charges and tenant payments, running move-outs, voiding bills, and running work orders. The published documentation shows no way to void or reverse a posted charge or payment, record a returned (NSF) payment, apply or refund a security deposit, post a journal entry, or run a full bank reconciliation. That puts coverage at 83.3%, just under the 85% an A needs.

mcp.note: Rentvine runs an official, vendor-hosted MCP server at mcp.rentvine.ai that reads and acts on account data and has been available to every customer since Oct 22, 2026, so the one-step bump applied: 85 (B) to 87 (B+).

reads.c2: The API is easy to call and page through, shows your rate-limit budget on every response, and has export endpoints that return only what changed. Build defensively, though. Values come back as text and inconsistently typed, and errors lack codes. The published documentation shows nothing that stops a retried payment from posting twice or one tool from overwriting another's edit, and no versioning promise.
reads.c3: You can give each app or AI agent its own key, limited to exactly the permissions it needs, and rotate or delete it yourself. AI assistants connect by signing in, not by pasting a key. The published documentation shows no test environment, so automations get tested against a live account.
reads.c4: A developer or AI coding tool can load the OpenAPI file and get most of the way. A few create endpoints are under-documented. There is no AI-ready copy of the API docs, and no API changelog warns you when something changes.

checks.title: Object coverage
checks.why: Objects earn 40.0 of 46 weight. Every object is at least partly covered; the general ledger, bank accounts, reconciliation, security deposits, files, and inventory are partial.

checks.title: Write coverage
checks.why: Both write workflows are fully documented: posting lease charges and payments, and creating and updating leases (6 of 6 weight).

checks.title: Lifecycle coverage
checks.why: Lifecycle actions earn 8.5 of 14 weight. Move-outs, voiding bills, and deactivating records are documented. The published documentation shows no way to void a posted charge or record a returned payment.

checks.title: Change notification
checks.why: Visible webhook events cover only work orders, leases, and properties being created or updated, with no full event list published. A documented changed-since filter with paging covers the main records and worked in live tests.

checks.title: Modern API conventions
checks.why: A resource-based REST API over JSON with an OpenAPI 3.1 spec. Using POST for updates and DELETE for voids is an accepted convention.

checks.title: Consistent typing
checks.why: Types vary across the API. IDs are sometimes numbers and sometimes text, yes/no flags come in three forms, and money is mostly text but sometimes a floating-point number.

checks.title: Structured errors
checks.why: Errors carry a usable message but no stable machine-readable code, and error shapes varied in live tests. One bad request returned a server error with an empty body.

checks.title: Duplicate prevention
checks.why: The published documentation shows no idempotency key or similar protection, so a retried charge, payment, bill, or deposit could post twice.

checks.title: Graceful handling under load
checks.why: Rate-limit headers showing account, user, and key quotas appear on normal responses. The published documentation shows no 429, Retry-After, or backoff guidance.

checks.title: Pagination for large collections
checks.why: Page and page-size paging with total counts works. Most lists have no stable sort order, the maximum page size is unpublished, and the next-page header misbehaved in live tests.

checks.title: Bulk or incremental export
checks.why: Export endpoints for leases, properties, units, and applications, plus a documented changed-since filter with paging on 17 operations. Both worked in live tests.

checks.title: Webhook security and delivery reliability
checks.why: A resettable signing key signs webhook payloads. The published documentation shows no signature format, retry policy, or replay guidance.

checks.title: Concurrency and conflict control
checks.why: The published documentation shows no way to stop one tool from silently overwriting another tool's edit.

checks.title: Versioning and backward compatibility
checks.why: There is no version number in the path or headers and no deprecation policy, and the terms allow API changes with or without notice.

checks.title: Request traceability
checks.why: The published documentation shows no Rentvine request ID. The only per-request ID comes from Amazon CloudFront, is undocumented, and is not shown to be usable with support.

checks.title: Service availability and status transparency
checks.why: A public status page has an API component, incident history with feeds, and uptime history (100% from September to November 2026). No SLA is published, which yes does not require.

checks.title: Read-only credentials
checks.why: Each key gets a role built from per-action permission toggles. A role with no modify permissions gives a read-only key.

checks.title: Scoped credentials
checks.why: Keys inherit fine-grained action permissions from their role and can be tied to a pod. Rentvine recommends least privilege.

checks.title: Multiple keys
checks.why: You can create multiple named keys and manage each one separately.

checks.title: Rotation and revocation
checks.why: You can regenerate a key's secret, change its role, or delete it yourself.

checks.title: Test environment and isolation
checks.why: The published documentation shows no sandbox, test mode, or test account, so automations get tested against live data.

checks.title: Delegated access
checks.why: The official MCP connector uses OAuth sign-in with read and write scopes, per-tool approval, and token revocation. The REST API itself uses only key-and-secret logins.

checks.title: Complete self-serve reference
checks.why: A public reference covers 205 operations with auth steps, parameters, and response examples. Some create calls list no request fields, webhooks are missing, and there is no error-code list.

checks.title: Reliable machine-consumable integration path
checks.why: A downloadable OpenAPI 3.1 spec covers all 205 operations. The official MCP connector is another path. There are no official SDKs.

checks.title: AI-readable documentation
checks.why: Rentvine's llms.txt files cover marketing and help articles, not the API. The docs site's llms.txt is blocked, and there is no documentation-search MCP.

checks.title: Kept current
checks.why: The published documentation shows no API changelog. Release notes are product-level and none mentions an API change, and the spec has stayed at version 1.0.0.

checks.title: Self-serve API key
checks.why: Customers create keys themselves in Settings, with no special approval from Rentvine.

checks.title: Not commercially gated
checks.why: The API and the MCP connector are included at no extra charge, and the MCP is free with every plan. A Claude or ChatGPT subscription is a separate third-party cost.

disagreements.why: The yes definition accepts a documented changed-since filter with paging, which Rentvine documents on 17 operations and which worked live. Run 1 read the check as needing a dedicated export path.

The methodology says an official hosted MCP with OAuth sign-in and approved scopes qualifies, and Rentvine's does. Run 1's concern about no documented Rentvine screen for revoking grants did not outweigh that rule.
There is no API changelog, the release notes never mention an API change, and the spec has no change history. Run 3 counted product release notes and an MCP activity note as thin currency signals.

runs.summary: All three runs scored 87 (B+), or 85 (B) before the MCP step, and scored all 32 checklist items the same. Every combination of the three disputed marks still gives 85 before the MCP step and 87 after it.

sensitivity: Capability coverage is 1.15 weight points short of the 85% an A needs, so a documented write path for the general ledger (journal entries) or bank accounts would lift the score from 85 (B) to 93 (A) before the MCP step and 97 (A+) after it.

bottom: Rentvine is property-management software with its own trust accounting, not a bank, and every customer gets its API and official AI (MCP) connector at no extra cost, using keys they create themselves. You can build automations that read almost everything, create leases, post charges and payments, run move-outs, and manage work orders, bills, and tenant messages, with each key limited to exactly what that tool needs. The weak spots are engineering polish and accounting corrections: the published documentation shows no protection against double-posting on retries, no versioning promise, no test environment, and no way to reverse ledger entries, record returned payments, refund deposits, or reconcile a full bank statement. Values also come back as inconsistently typed text, so build carefully. You still need your own bank for the trust accounts, and those corrections stay inside the Rentvine app. Rentvine is 1.15 weight points short of an A, and a documented write path for journal entries or bank accounts would move it to 97 (A+).
provider_fit: Rentvine is cloud property-management software with built-in trust accounting, not a bank, priced per active unit with the API and MCP connector included. You still need your own bank for the trust accounts, plus a webhook receiver or polling job to react to changes.
